lines.text: Two beams meet end to end, each cut away to about half its width. The upper piece is lowered from above, and two hardwood pegs are driven in from the sides.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: This is the okkake daisen-tsugi. One English glossary describes it as an oblique, housed and rabbeted scarf joint.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress. Say 'okkake daisen-tsugi' as o-k-ka-ke (a short pause on the double k), dai-sen, tsu-gi: short, even syllables, hard g. The last word is 'tsugi': start it with a clear 'ts' sound, as in 'tsunami', never 'sugi'.

lines.text: Japanese references read it okkake daisen-tsugi. Daisen is written with the characters for large and peg. Without the pegs, the same joint is called okkake-tsugi.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Say 'okkake daisen-tsugi' as o-k-ka-ke (a short pause on the double k), dai-sen, tsu-gi: short, even syllables, hard g. Say 'dai-sen' as two short syllables. The last word is 'tsugi': start it with a clear 'ts' sound, as in 'tsunami', never 'sugi'.

lines.text: In episode nine, the Flat 35 house specification offered two splices for the beams in the outer walls at second-floor level: the gooseneck, or this one.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Unlike the gooseneck, the two pieces aren't different shapes. Both are the same shape, turned end for end, though one training course warns that the slope runs the other way on the upper piece. They're called the lower piece and the upper piece: the lower piece is set first, and the upper piece is lowered onto it.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Over the splice, each piece keeps about half the width, but its full depth. Seen from above, the joint line runs along the beam, with a step at the middle, the ago, and a small tongue at each end, the mechigai.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress. Say 'ah-go' as two short syllables, and 'meh-chee-guy' as me-chi-gai, short and even.
lines.tts: Over the splice, each piece keeps about half the width, but its full depth. Seen from above, the joint line runs along the beam, with a step at the middle, the ah-go, and a small tongue at each end, the meh-chee-guy.

lines.text: The step at the middle has a slight slope. As the upper piece is lowered, the slope draws the two pieces together along the beam, until the end shoulders close up tight.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Then two pegs go in through the side faces, from opposite sides. They stop the joint lifting back out. It's the slope, not the pegs, that the sources credit with drawing it tight.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: In our model, without the pegs it can't be pulled apart or pushed sideways, but it can lift straight out. With the pegs in, it can't.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The Flat 35 specification offers it for those outer-wall beams, for eaves plates, and for one option on second-floor floor beams. For roof beams it's the first choice; the gooseneck is allowed only where the beam is about a hundred and twenty millimeters deep, and then with steel straps and bolts.

lines.text: None of those clauses names hardware for this splice. As in each of them, it's placed off the post, a short way out along the beam.

lines.text: How long should it be? A carpenters' training course says about three times the depth gives the most strength, and a joinery handbook gives three to four times for beams a hundred and five or a hundred and twenty millimeters deep. One test database suggests one and a half to three times.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 115 words per minute, unhurried, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Our model uses one laboratory's test proportions: a beam a hundred and twenty millimeters wide and a hundred and eighty deep, with a splice twice the depth.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: In that lab's tests, at the same depth, these splices held two to three and a half times the pull of its gooseneck specimens, though they were also much longer. Again, the depth of the beam mattered more than the length of the splice.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: It resists bending better than the gooseneck, but only partly. The test database notes it's often treated as a pin in design.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: And it's slow to cut by hand, because the two pieces are fitted against each other. One architect's guide reports one to four splices per person per day.
